name: PCF85363ATT_AJ
title: PCF85363A: real-time clock and calendar with stop-watch, two alarms, three timestamps, battery switch-over, 64 byte RAM and I²C-bus
summary: A CMOS clock and calendar counting from hundredths of a second to years, running from an external 32.768 kHz quartz with on-chip load capacitors selectable for 6, 7 or 12.5 pF crystals. Instead of a calendar it can count elapsed time up to 999 999 hours. Around the counter sit two alarms, a watchdog, a periodic interrupt, three timestamp registers fed by the TS pin or by supply changes, a digital offset trim, a programmable clock output and two interrupt outputs. A built-in switch moves the chip onto a backup cell at VBAT when VDD fails, keeping the time and the 64 byte RAM. The clock keeps running down to 0.9 V and draws 280 nA typical at 3.3 V; the 400 kHz I²C interface needs 1.8 V or more. Three packages: DFN2626-10 (PCF85363ATL), TSSOP8 (PCF85363ATT) and TSSOP10 (PCF85363ATT1).
key_figures: 1.8 V to 5.5 V at fSCL = 400 kHz
0.28 μA typ at VDD = 3.0 V, 25 °C; 280 nA typ, 420 nA max at 3.3 V, 25 °C, battery switch off; 320 nA typ with it on
I²C-bus, 400 kHz, address A2h write / A3h read
32.768 kHz quartz, CL 6 pF, 7 pF or 12.5 pF, RS up to 100 kΩ (normal drive)
32 768 Hz down to 1 Hz on CLK, TS or INTA
64 bytes plus one single byte, battery backed

notes: DFN2626-10: 2.6 x 2.6 x 0.5 mm body, 0.5 mm pitch, 10 terminals, thermally enhanced. TSSOP8: 3 mm body width, 0.65 mm pitch. TSSOP10: 3 mm body width, 0.5 mm pitch.
PCF85363ATT1/AJ is discontinued (notice 202104010DN, PCN 202104008A); PCF85363ATT1/AZ replaces it drop-in.
SSB packing ships in a static shielding bag; parts stay sealed in it between uses.
The TSSOP8 part has no TS and no CLK pin. The PCF85363ATL carries UL component recognition.

circuits.title: Typical application with battery backup and I²C host
circuits.description: The clock sits on an I²C bus beside a host controller, both fed from VDD. A 32.768 kHz quartz across OSCI and OSCO sets the time base. A backup cell on VBAT, with its own 100 nF capacitor, takes over when VDD drops; VDD has a 100 nF capacitor of its own. SDA and SCL each have a pull-up to VDD sized from the wanted rise time and the bus capacitance (R = tr / Cb), and the open-drain INTA output has its own pull-up to VDD. CLK delivers the square-wave clock output, and a switch from TS to ground gives a timestamp or start/stop input.

parts.note: quartz; data taken with ESR 60 kΩ

notes: CLK and TS exist on the DFN2626-10 and TSSOP10 parts only.
A crystal with 70 kΩ ESR instead of 60 kΩ raises the current by a few nA and lengthens start-up a little.

equations.expr: Offset value = Eppm / 2.17 (OFFM = 0); Offset value = Eppm / 2.0345 (OFFM = 1)
equations.note: Example: 3.926 (OFFM = 0) and 4.188 (OFFM = 1), so 4 correction pulses either way. Four pulses are -8.680 ppm in normal mode and -8.138 ppm in fast mode, leaving -0.160 ppm and +0.382 ppm. The trim reaches ±1 ppm, half a step, which is 0.0864 s per day.

operation.text: All registers are 8 bits wide, though not every bit exists. The address pointer steps up by one after every byte read or written. In the time and control block it runs from 00h to 2Fh and then returns to 00h; inside the RAM, 40h to 7Fh, it returns from 7Fh to 40h.

Reading any time register freezes a copy of all the counters, so a carry cannot split a reading; counting carries on underneath. The whole set, 100th seconds up to years (or up to HR_00_xx_xx in stop-watch mode), is read or written in a single I²C transfer; splitting it over two transfers lets the time roll over between them and corrupts the result.

Start a transfer at 2Eh, write 01h to set STOP, then A4h to clear the prescaler; the pointer has rolled over to 00h, so the time bytes follow, 100th seconds to years. End the transfer. When the outside reference says go, write 00h to 2Eh: counting starts. In stop-watch mode the same sequence with all-zero time bytes resets the watch. Example for 14:23:19: A2h, 2Eh, 01h, A4h, 00h, 19h, 23h, 14h... then later A2h, 2Eh, 00h.

The stop signal (STOP bit, or the TS pin when STOPM allows it) gates the 8.192 kHz clock behind the 32 768 Hz oscillator and freezes the counters; the clock outputs keep running. Because the release is asynchronous to the oscillator, the first count comes 0 µs to 122 µs after STOP is released.

OS, bit 7 of Seconds, is set whenever the oscillator is not running, including from power-on until the quartz has settled, which takes 200 ms to 2 s depending on the crystal, temperature and supply. It stays set until software clears it; if clearing does not stick, the oscillator is still stopped. Watching OS therefore shows whether the supply has fallen too low to oscillate.
EMON, bit 7 of Minutes, reads 1 while any bit in the Flags register is set and 0 once all are clear. It is read-only.

With RTCM = 1 the counter becomes an elapsed-time counter from 0.01 s to 999 999 hours in BCD, hours held across three registers; there are no day, weekday, month or year registers, and 12_24 has no effect. Reset state is 00 00 00:00:00.00 with OS = 1 and EMON = 0.

With 100TH set, the 100th_seconds register counts at 0.01 s resolution. The 100 Hz tick comes from 256 Hz divided by 3 for fourteen periods and by 2 for eleven, an average of 2.56; single ticks jitter up to 3.91 ms, with no error left over each 25 ticks.

Two alarms, each with its own enable bit per field. In RTC mode alarm 1 matches seconds, minutes, hours, day and month, and alarm 2 minutes, hours and weekday; in stop-watch mode alarm 1 covers seconds up to 999 999 hours and alarm 2 minutes up to 9 999 hours. Only fields whose enable bit is 1 are compared; unused alarm registers need not be written. When the time steps onto a match of all enabled fields, A1F or A2F is set; it is not set again merely because the match persists. Flags stay set until cleared. In pulse mode a fresh pulse appears at every new match even if the flag was left set.

A 5-bit down-counter loaded with WDR[4:0], 1 to 31; writing 0 stops it, writing any other value starts it at once, even mid-period. Steps are 4 s, 1 s, 1/4 s or 1/16 s, giving 62.5 ms to 124 s; for longer intervals an alarm serves. Because loading is asynchronous to the watchdog clock the first period may be one step short; later periods are exact. Reading returns the live count, which cannot be frozen, so read twice and compare. In repeat mode the counter reloads itself at the end of each period and sets WDF; in single-shot mode it stops at 0 with WDF set and must be reloaded. WDF clears only by command.

Three read-only timestamp registers copy the time, in the format of the current mode, on chosen events: TSR1 on TS pin events, TSR3 on battery switch-over events, TSR2 on either. A first-event mode records once and then waits until its flag is cleared; a last-event mode records every event without needing the flag cleared. Each update sets TSRnF and can raise an interrupt whatever the flag state. CTS clears all three registers. In battery operation the mechanical switch detector can still trigger them.

OFFSET[7:0] in two's complement adds or removes clock pulses; the oscillator frequency itself does not change, only the length of some seconds. Normal mode (OFFM = 0) acts once every 4 hours, one pulse per minute until the count is done, 2.170 ppm per step; fast mode (OFFM = 1) acts every 8 minutes, one pulse per second, 2.0345 ppm per step, at a higher current. The register serves accuracy tuning, aging adjustment and temperature compensation; fast mode suits dynamic correction such as temperature compensation. Each correction pulse can raise a pulse interrupt (OIEA/OIEB); there is no flag for it. The 1 Hz clock output and the periodic interrupt are not affected.

INTA (open-drain, INTA pin) and INTB (push-pull, on the TS pin with TSPM[1:0] = 01) take the same sources, chosen independently in INTA_enable and INTB_enable; both are active LOW and appear only once the pin mode is set. INTB works only while on VDD; INTA works on VDD and VBAT. In pulse mode (ILPx = 0) each trigger gives a pulse ended by an internal 128 Hz clock, so it lasts one to two 128 Hz periods, or less if the flag is cleared first. Triggers: each elapsed period, each correction pulse, each alarm match, each timestamp update, each switch to or from battery, each watchdog expiry. In level mode (ILPx = 1) the pin follows the enabled flags and releases only when all of them are cleared.

Every flag is set by its function and stays set until written to 0. A write ANDs the byte into the register, so writing 1 to the other bits leaves them as they were and each flag can be cleared alone.

PI[1:0] gives a pulse every second, minute or hour and sets PIF. Turning it off resets its timer; after turning it on, the first pulse comes between one period and one period less 1 s. It ignores STOP and offset correction, and needs no flag clearing between pulses.

CL[1:0] selects on-chip load capacitance for 6.0 pF, 7.0 pF or 12.5 pF crystals; with the match right the frequency offset is zero, the setting allowing for some package and board stray capacitance. 12.5 pF crystals are the cheapest and commonest but take the most current. A 9.0 pF crystal also works with CL set to 7.0 pF plus offset calibration. Normal drive covers crystals up to 100 kΩ series resistance (ESR); low drive, up to 60 kΩ, saves current; high drive, up to 500 kΩ, costs much more current.

COF[2:0] selects 32 768 Hz down to 1 Hz, or off, for CLK (push-pull, on at power-on), and for TS or INTA when they are set to clock mode. CLKPM = 1 turns CLK off and drives it LOW. Every frequency but 32 768 Hz is 50:50. CLKIV inverts the output, except for COF = 111. LOWJ halves jitter (50 ns to 25 ns typ) at extra current, on the rising edge, or on the falling edge with CLKIV set, which suits an open-drain output. INTA comes out of reset as a 32 kHz clock: to save power, set COF to off when no clock is needed, or move INTA to interrupt or battery-mode use when only CLK is wanted.

The switch compares VDD with an internal threshold Vth (1.5 V or 2.8 V by BSTH), with VBAT, with the higher of the two, or with the lower (BSM[1:0]); comparing with both Vth and VBAT suits a rechargeable cell. Switching has hysteresis. Going to battery sets BSF and can give an interrupt or a static LOW on INTA; going back to VDD can give a pulse. On battery the VDD domain is off: I²C, digital TS input and the TS output modes are disabled, CLK is Hi-Z, and SCL, SDA and a digital TS input may float; the TS mechanical switch detector and INTA interrupt and battery indication stay active, INTA clock output does not. BSF can be read only once back on VDD. BSOFF = 1 turns the switch off to save current; VBAT is then tied to VDD.

With TSPM[1:0] = 11 the TS pin is an input, active HIGH or LOW by TSL, for timestamps and, with STOPM = 1, for starting and stopping the count. TSIM = 0 makes it a CMOS input referred to VDD, ignored and free to float on battery. TSIM = 1 makes it a mechanical-switch sensor: every 1/16 s, for 30.5 µs, a pull-up of 80 kΩ or 40 kΩ (TSPULL) is switched on and the pin sampled against the internal supply, working on VDD and VBAT. The 40 kΩ value helps with a long cable or large capacitance but draws more while the switch is closed. With 00 it floats at Hi-Z and needs no defined level.

INTAPM[1:0] chooses clock output (00, reset state, VDD only, Hi-Z on battery), battery-mode indication (01: Hi-Z on VDD, LOW on VBAT, working on both), INTA interrupts (10, active LOW, on VDD and VBAT) or Hi-Z (11). The output is open-drain in every mode.
Power-on generates a reset, and writing 2Ch to register 2Fh repeats it, including CPR and CTS. Alarm registers keep their contents; everything else returns to the reset values.
64 bytes at 40h to 7Fh plus the single byte at 2Ch hold any data. They are readable and writable on VDD and keep their contents on VBAT, when the interface is off.

A two-wire target at 1010 001 (A2h write, A3h read); both lines need pull-ups to the supply. A write sends the register address, 00h to 2Fh, then any number of data bytes, the pointer stepping after each and wrapping from 2Fh to 00h; an address outside that range is acknowledged but the transfer is ignored. A read starts at the current pointer, which a short write sets first; the controller acknowledges each byte and ends with a not-acknowledge before STOP or a repeated START. The interface is unavailable on VBAT, and one access, START to START or STOP, must take under one second.

operation.topic: Stop-watch with a switch on TS
operation.text: Example use: stop-watch mode as an elapsed-time counter started and stopped by a mechanical switch from TS to VSS. With the settings in the register table, closing the switch pulls TS LOW; on the next 16 Hz sample the LOW is seen, counting stops, TSR2 takes the time and TSR2F is set, and INTA gives a pulse. Opening the switch lets the pull-up lift TS to the internal supply and counting resumes at the next sample. The sampler holds a stale level until mechanical-switch mode is on and needs one sample period to settle, so enable that mode at least 62.5 ms before the timestamp event mode to avoid a false first event.

The die pad connects to VSS only through high-ohmic attach and is treated as isolated. Soldering it to an isolated copper pad helps heat flow but is not needed at this power level; keep traces out from under it.
Inputs and input/outputs are held at VSS or VDD unless a mode allows them to float; VBAT goes to VDD when no backup is used.
Parts are stored at +8 °C to +45 °C and 25 % to 75 % humidity.
